data.title: Behind the $21 billion valuation: Why Nasdaq is heavily tying itself to Kraken.
data.description:
Written by: Shannon@Jinse Finance On September 10th, according to Bloomberg, Nasdaq Ventures, the strategic investment arm of Nasdaq Inc., will invest $100 million in Payward, the parent company of cryptocurrency exchange Kraken. This round of investment brings Payward's valuation to $21 billion. This is not the first collaboration between Nasdaq and Payward. In March of this year, the two companies announced a joint development of an infrastructure connecting regulated stock markets and blockchain networks, namely the "Nasdaq Equity Tokens" (NET) project. This $100 million equity investment marks an upgrade in their relationship from simple business cooperation to a capital commitment. According to the details of the cooperation disclosed by both parties, this deepened cooperation mainly includes three aspects: 1. Tokenized Stock Distribution: Kraken will provide users with tokenized stocks of Nasdaq-listed companies, and these tokens are designed to have the same voting rights as ordinary shares. This is a feature not currently available in most tokenized stock products on the market; previous similar products typically only granted holders price exposure without shareholder rights. 2. Market Surveillance Technology Introduction: Payward will introduce Nasdaq's market surveillance technology into all its trading venues, including cryptocurrencies, stocks, tokenized stocks, and futures and options, to strengthen trading compliance and market integrity. 3. Settlement Infrastructure: Payward's already operating tokenized stock product, xStocks, will serve as the main settlement layer for the NET system. It has been disclosed that xStocks has accumulated a trading volume exceeding $25 billion, with over 85,000 independent holders. Nasdaq plans to officially launch the NET product in the second quarter of 2027. This timeline builds upon its rule amendment application submitted to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) last year. This application aimed to allow stocks to be traded in tokenized form on regulated exchanges and was approved in March of this year. Why Kraken? For Nasdaq, choosing Payward was no accident. As one of the world's oldest cryptocurrency exchanges, Kraken's strategic focus in recent years has shifted from simple cryptocurrency trading to building a comprehensive infrastructure spanning traditional finance and on-chain assets. Its xStocks product packages U.S. stocks and ETFs into tokenized assets that can be freely transferred and traded on the blockchain, allowing users to bypass centralized exchanges and directly bring these assets into on-chain wallets and the DeFi ecosystem. This ability to "put traditional assets on-chain" is precisely the piece of the puzzle that Nasdaq needs most when building its own tokenization system. A partner that has already successfully implemented on-chain distribution, settlement, and user growth can significantly shorten the timeline from regulatory approval to product launch for Nasdaq. It's worth noting that Payward's recent fundraising and partnership activities have been quite frequent. In April, Deutsche Börse invested approximately $200 million in Payward, acquiring about 1.5% of its equity; in early September, Payward also partnered with the London Stock Exchange Group (LSE) to introduce tokenized UK stocks to investors in 2027. This means that Payward is simultaneously building a network of partnerships with several leading global exchanges for tokenized assets, acting more like a "middle-layer" infrastructure provider connecting regulated markets in different jurisdictions with the blockchain world, rather than simply a cryptocurrency exchange. Competitive Landscape: A Battle with the NYSE Nasdaq's increased investment can also be seen as a direct response to its long-time rival, the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE). In March of this year, Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), the parent company of the NYSE, made a strategic investment of approximately $200 million in cryptocurrency exchange OKX at a valuation of approximately $25 billion, and obtained a board seat. The cooperation covers tokenized stocks, crypto futures, clearing and custody, and cross-market trading infrastructure. By June, ICE and OKX had further established a 50/50 joint venture, planning to tokenize NYSE-listed assets and open them to OKX's global users for trading, while simultaneously applying for US broker-dealer and futures commission merchant (FCM) licenses. Thus, two parallel "stock tokenization" camps have formed between the world's two largest traditional securities exchanges and the two largest cryptocurrency exchanges: Nasdaq + Kraken/Payward versus NYSE/ICE + OKX. The core of this competition lies in who can be the first to scale up and bring "24/7, programmable, and cross-border transferable" stock token products to the market within a compliant framework, thereby seizing the dominant infrastructure position in the migration of the traditional securities settlement system to on-chain. Why are tokenized stocks attractive? Payward co-CEO Arjun Sethi, when discussing this collaboration, mentioned a compelling industry pain point: Currently, over $2 trillion in stock transactions in the US need to be processed through the clearing system daily. The net settlement ratio between buyers and sellers is approximately 98%, but clearinghouses still need to hold $10 billion to $20 billion in collateral for the remaining transactions and wait one day for settlement. In 2024 alone, shortening the settlement cycle from two days to one day freed up approximately $3 billion in tied-up funds. This data reveals the core cost of the traditional securities settlement system. There is a time lag between trading and actual fund/securities settlement, and this time lag requires real-money collateral to cover the risk exposure. If on-chain instant settlement is achieved through blockchain, this waiting period can theoretically be eliminated, further freeing up the efficiency of funds tied up in collateral. This is also the fundamental business logic behind traditional exchanges like Nasdaq and the NYSE's willingness to invest resources in tokenization. It's not about chasing the speculative hype of cryptocurrencies, but about focusing on an efficiency revolution in settlement infrastructure. Furthermore, the design that "token holders enjoy the same voting rights as ordinary shareholders" is a crucial but often overlooked aspect of this collaboration. Previously, most tokenized stock products on the market were essentially just synthetic assets or derivative certificates tracking stock prices; holders did not truly possess shareholder rights. If the NET project truly achieves a one-to-one correspondence between token voting rights and off-chain shareholder rights, it will mean that tokenized stocks are moving closer to "real stocks" in terms of law and governance. This will also bring new technical and compliance challenges to the shareholder structure management and proxy voting processes of listed companies.

Regulatory Path and Practical Constraints

It is important to emphasize that Nasdaq's series of actions are not free experiments in a regulatory vacuum, but rather based on communication with the SEC and obtaining rule exemptions.

Last year, Nasdaq's rule amendment application submitted to the SEC had the core demand of allowing stocks to be traded in tokenized form on "regulated trading venues." This means that tokenization does not mean escaping the existing securities regulatory framework, but rather, while preserving issuer control, the existing regulatory system, and shareholder rights, it gives stocks the programmability and circulation efficiency of the blockchain layer.

This "in-regulation tokenization" path is significantly different from a pure DeFi narrative. Nasdaq has repeatedly emphasized that its token design aims to "preserve issuer control" and plans to uniformly deploy market monitoring technology across all its trading venues (covering cryptocurrencies, stocks, tokenized stocks, futures, and options). Essentially, this involves integrating blockchain technology into the existing securities regulation, clearing and custody, and market integrity systems, rather than circumventing them.

However, there is still a long way to go from announcing the partnership to actually launching the product. The target timeline of Q2 2027 means that there is about a year and a half left for infrastructure development, cross-institutional testing, and regulatory communication. Meanwhile, it is worth noting that Nasdaq's strategic investment is also considered to have further delayed Payward's original plans for an initial public offering (IPO). With the funding and strategic backing of a traditional exchange, Payward's urgency in the capital markets has decreased, and its IPO timeline has reportedly been postponed to after Q2 2027. What does this mean? Looking at this event within a broader industry context, several clear trend lines are converging. Firstly, traditional financial infrastructure giants are viewing "equity tokenization" as a crucial battleground for the next generation of market structures. Whether it's Nasdaq partnering with Kraken/Payward, or the NYSE/ICE partnering with OKX, the common logic is to dominate the issuance, distribution, trading, and settlement standards of tokenized assets within a regulated framework, rather than completely ceding this field to purely cryptocurrency-native participants. Secondly, crypto exchanges are undergoing a transformation from "speculative venues" to "financial infrastructure providers." Leading exchanges like Kraken/Payward and OKX have received substantial equity investments from traditional financial institutions (Nasdaq, Deutsche Börse, ICE, etc.) in the past two years, essentially integrating them into the supply chain of traditional capital markets. Their valuation logic is now more aligned with infrastructure companies than simply trading platforms. Thirdly, tokenization is no longer just about "replicating a stock price with blockchain," but is beginning to touch upon deeper market structure issues such as settlement efficiency, shareholder rights, and regulatory compliance. Equal voting rights, unified market monitoring, and shortened clearing and settlement cycles—these details all point to a larger issue: the underlying rails of the securities market are being redesigned. For ordinary investors, in the short term, this event is more of a signal at the capital market level and will not immediately change their daily trading experience. However, in the medium to long term, if the tokenized stock systems led by Nasdaq and the NYSE are implemented as scheduled around 2027, the way investors buy and sell US stocks, settlement times, and even the convenience of cross-border asset transfers may undergo substantial changes. This "stock tokenization race," led by traditional Wall Street giants and deeply involved in cryptocurrency exchanges, may have only just begun.

data.title: Even without the Clarity Act, the US crypto regulatory framework is becoming increasingly clear.
data.description:
Source: Zach Pandl, Head of Research at Grayscale; Translated by: Jinse Finance Claw

The CLARITY Act, a bipartisan legislative proposal aimed at establishing a comprehensive set of rules for the cryptocurrency market, will face a crucial test in the Senate on September 15th: a vote to end debate on whether the bill should proceed to the full Senate. This vote requires the support of 60 senators to pass. Currently, Republicans hold 53 seats in the Senate, so the bill's progress requires Democratic support. The market predicts that the bill has a low probability of passing in 2026, reflecting policy divisions and a tight legislative schedule. If the motion to end the debate fails to pass, the path to passage this year will be even more remote. However, lawmakers can reconsider the bill during a lame-duck session or in a future Congress. Nevertheless, the CLARITY Act is no longer the only source of regulatory guidance. Even without the CLARITY Act, the U.S. regulatory framework for stablecoins, token issuance, tokenized securities, and perpetual futures is becoming increasingly clear (see Chart 1). 1. The GENIUS Act has established a federal framework for payments of stablecoins. 2. The U.S. SEC's proposed "Regulation Crypto Assets" will open clearer pathways for token financing, while potential innovation exemptions could allow certain securities market activities to move on-chain. 3. The U.S. SEC's proposed transfer agent rule would allow the blockchain to serve as the official record of ownership for issuers, further supporting tokenization. 4. The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has also opened regulated U.S. channels for perpetual futures through Kalshi and Coinbase, potentially paving the way for products associated with platforms like Hyperliquid. A clear division remains crucial, as only Congress can establish a comprehensive and lasting separation of powers between the U.S. SEC and the CFTC. Even if a consensus isn't reached in 2026, it won't hinder the progress already made in the regulatory arena. Key takeaway: CLARITY will provide the most comprehensive framework for the US cryptocurrency market, but its passage is not decisive—crypto policy is already progressing and offers better clarity in several other areas. Chart 1: US cryptocurrency regulation has moved beyond the CLARITY Act and will continue to move forward.

data.title: What you thought was a security compliance check turned out to be handing your assets over to hackers.
data.description:
Foreword

Have you ever encountered this situation: You want to check if your wallet address has any "dark history," and you find an "AML checker." The interface looks very professional, with a progress bar, compliance verification indicators, and even the words "FATF regulated." You connect your wallet, click scan, and the system prompts you to pay a "verification fee." You do so, and then see a green "Clean, Low Risk" result, and breathe a sigh of relief.

A few months later, you find that the assets in your wallet have been wiped out.

This is not alarmist. On August 19, 2026, cybersecurity company Malwarebytes disclosed that a large number of fake anti-money laundering (AML) check websites are actively operating, tricking users into connecting their wallets and signing malicious transactions, directly emptying their account assets.

This is not an exaggeration. On August 19, 2026, cybersecurity company Malwarebytes disclosed that a large number of fake anti-money laundering (AML) check websites are actively operating, tricking users into connecting their wallets and signing malicious transactions, directly wiping out their account assets.

... Some websites impersonate the well-known compliance service AMLBot, while others use generic names like "AML Check," but in essence, they are just the same malicious template being repeatedly packaged and used. The real irony is: you think you're conducting a security compliance check, but you're actually handing your wallet over to hackers. In short: scammers exploit your anxiety about "regulatory compliance," packaging their scams as "security checks." Anti-money laundering (AML) screening is already a familiar concept in the cryptocurrency world. Exchanges, custodians, and DeFi platforms often use it to screen wallet addresses for links to hacks, theft, sanctions, or other suspicious activities. As compliance tools become more widely known to ordinary users, opportunities for scammers arise. The sophistication of these scams lies in three psychological tactics: 1. Creating Compliance Anxiety: Scammers make you believe that "not checking might be a violation." Under the DAC8 directive and the MiCA compliance wave, users have developed a conditioned reflex to "compliance checks." Fake websites exploit this psychology, making you feel that "this should be a normal process." 2. Disguising It as a Security Tool: A tool claiming to "check if your money is legal" sounds much more credible than "high-yield investments." "People use AML checkers to protect themselves. Scammers exploit this caution, packaging each step as a legitimate security check," wrote researchers at Malwarebytes. The process involves progress bars, compliance verification messages, and fake error messages requesting small deposits, culminating in a reassuring "Clean, Low Risk" conclusion. The entire process appears highly professional, making it difficult for ordinary users to detect the deception immediately. The images above show genuine and fake AMLBot websites, respectively, attempting to lure users into "connecting their wallets" for so-called "security checks." Legitimate AML screening only requires a public wallet address; any tool that asks for a "wallet connection" should be treated with extreme caution. Part 02 - The Core Difference Between Genuine and Fake AML Checks In short: Genuine AML checks only require your public address; fake ones insist on you "connecting your wallet." Cryptocurrency anti-money laundering screening is essentially a read-only query: it uses a wallet address to check transaction records on the blockchain to see if there are any connections to sanctioned addresses, hacked attacks, or fraudulent funds. This operation only requires providing a publicly available receiving address; it does not require wallet connection, authorization, signature, or any fees. Fake websites are the opposite. Researchers at Malwarebytes explicitly state: "If an AML inspector asks you to connect your wallet instead of simply entering its public address, treat it as a warning sign." The key difference is obvious: Connecting to a wallet doesn't inherently hand over your private key, but it exposes information about the assets in your wallet. An attacker can use this information to construct a "transaction" and then push it to the user for approval. Once the user clicks "approval," the attacker gains access to transfer the corresponding tokens in the wallet, and the assets are immediately emptied. Part 03 - The Five-Step Trap of Fake AML Website Attacks In short: The problem doesn't occur the moment you connect your wallet; the money only leaves after you click "Approve." One attack process recorded by Malwarebytes is as follows: Step 1: Luring the Connection The user visits a fake website, sees a prompt to "select cryptocurrency and scan," and is asked to "connect your wallet to view the results." The interface looks identical to the real one. Step 2: Simulating a Scan The progress bar displays "Checking wallet history..." and "Verifying compliance...", creating the illusion that the system is working diligently. Step 3: Fake Error A fake error message pops up, requesting a small deposit to "pay for the testing fee." This design makes the user feel that "this is part of the normal process," rather than a suspicious operation. Step 4: Return "Safe" Result Regardless of whether the fee was actually paid, the system will ultimately display a "safe, low-risk" conclusion and provide the option to "download the report." The victim leaves reassured, while the attacker has already gained control of the wallet's transfer permissions through the approved operation. Step 5: Assets Empty The victim may not discover their wallet has been emptied for weeks or even months, or worse—they may never know. The core of the entire process isn't connecting the wallet itself, but rather clicking the "Approve" button after connecting. Malwarebytes points out that what's being approved is "token access permission"—once you sign the authorization, it's equivalent to giving the other party the key to your wallet, allowing for continuous asset transfers without secondary confirmation. Part 04 - Three Ironclad Rules to Protect Your Wallet In short: Remember these three ironclad rules, and don't let your guard down just because the interface looks professional. Rule One: Never connect your wallet for "checks". A legitimate AML check is essentially a read-only query of publicly available data—it can be completed simply by entering the wallet address. This is the most basic criterion and the core basis for distinguishing between genuine and fake checks. Any service that requires you to "connect your wallet to check," no matter how professional the interface or how realistic the logo, should be turned off immediately. **Rule Two: Beware of Requests to Pay Small Fees** Fake error messages → inducing small deposits → requesting fees → returning fake "safe" results—this is the standard operating procedure for scams. Genuine AML checks do not incur any fees. Any "security check" involving payment should be considered a clear risk signal. **Rule Three: Regularly Check and Revoke Authorizations** If you suspect you have visited a suspicious website, even without direct asset loss, you should check and revoke all unfamiliar authorizations in your wallet's authorization management interface. This only takes a few minutes but could prevent a potential loss of assets. If you have inadvertently approved a suspicious transaction, immediately transfer any remaining assets to a new wallet; the original wallet is no longer secure. This is the last line of defense to prevent further losses. The core logic is that attackers are not exploiting technical vulnerabilities, but rather users' ingrained trust in "compliance checks." Adhering to the three bottom lines of "not connecting wallets, not paying fees, and regularly checking authorizations" will help you avoid most of these traps. In conclusion, fake AML website attacks are the latest example of "trust being weaponized"—scammers no longer promise high returns, but instead exploit your anxiety about compliance and security itself. You intend to protect yourself, but you end up handing your wallet over to hackers. Remember these three ironclad rules: • AML checks do not require a wallet connection, only a public address. • No fees are required. • No transaction approval or authorization is needed. From April 2024 to January 2026, CoinDCX alone identified over 1,200 phishing websites impersonating legitimate platforms. In 2025, CertiK data shows that the crypto industry lost up to $3.3 billion due to malicious attacks. Compliance anxiety has become a new tool for scammers, and the way to spot it is actually quite simple: any AML tool that requires a wallet connection should be turned off immediately.
